answers.question: Is shipped DOI actually cited by the current report?
answers.answer: Yes. Deposited reference 3 identifies the exact title, journal, volume and pages; Crossref resolves the deposited reference to 10.1227/neu.0000000000003032. This advances citation identity, not finding-level retest attribution.

answers.question: Does 2024 versus 2025 designate another original paper?
answers.answer: The shipped DOI has electronic publication on 20 June 2024 and issue publication on 1 January 2025, volume 96(1), pages 142–151. The current deposited reference uses its 2025 issue year. These dates are consistent versions of that DOI; date difference alone supplies no additional report.

answers.question: What endpoints and sample sizes are actually reported?
answers.answer: Current abstract: 196 cadets assessed at preinjury baseline, within 48 hours, asymptomatic, and unrestricted activity. Its listed PLR measures include end-minus-initial diameter, constriction percentage, T75, maximum constriction velocity and average dilation velocity. Shipped original abstract: 1,300 baseline cadets, 68 incident mTBIs, the same broad assessment stages, changes in diameter difference/dilation velocity/constriction percentage, and a dilation-plus-maximum-constriction predictor of return before/after 21 days (AUC .71). Endpoint correspondence is observable; current recruitment dates, baseline denominator, exclusions and individual overlap are not.

answers.question: Is reference 10 an independent report or a companion analysis?
answers.answer: The full Focus report explicitly says it refines prior submitted/unpublished data and is a deeper analysis of previous work pending publication. It studies August 2021–December 2022, reports n=68 with 64 returning within 2 months and 4 later, and notes three >100-day cases excluded. Its stated previous 21-day dichotomized prediction closely corresponds to the shipped abstract. This is substantive primary evidence of a companion-analysis relationship, but the pending work is not named by title/DOI in those passages. Equivalence to the shipped report therefore remains a cross-source inference, not an explicit citation identity. It must not be counted as an independently retested original simply because it has another DOI.

answers.question: Does current N=196 establish a fresh cohort relative to original N=68?
answers.answer: No. Unequal reported sample sizes can reflect new recruitment, expansion, changed eligibility, additional follow-up or re-analysis. The current abstract and deposited references do not specify which occurred. No acquired current body/methods passage proves overlap, independence, or that all 196 are incident cases.

answers.question: Does recovered evidence establish an actual retest of the shipped finding, rather than related same-cohort work?
answers.answer: The current abstract claims replication generically, and its deposited references include the shipped report. No acquired current primary passage connects that claim to reference 3 rather than the other PLR empirical reports, and no acquired current methods passage establishes new data versus overlapping/expanded cohort analysis. A citation list plus matching measures does not settle this relationship. If current body explicitly links its new-data comparison to reference 3, the shipped identity can be evaluated against that passage; if it links another report, that report and possible equivalence need separate inspection.

quotes.quote: We were able to replicate the use of several PLR metrics as a biomarker for mTBI diagnosis that could easily be included with standard clinical measures.

One hundred and ninety-six US Military Academy cadets completed standard concussion assessments (Standardized Assessment of Concussion, Sport Concussion Assessment Tool-5, and Balance Error Scoring System) during accession for preinjury baseline and post-mTBI within 48 hours, when they were asymptomatic, and when they were cleared for unrestricted return to activity. At each of these time points, a handheld pupillometer was used to assess pupillary light reflex in both eyes consecutively.

PLR metrics that showed significant disruption (larger change, longer time, and faster velocity) at injury (T1) compared with baseline (T0) included overall diameter change (End-Initial_Diam, P < .001), the percent of pupil constriction (Constriction%, P < .01), the time for the pupil to return to 75% of its starting size (T75, P < .05), and the maximum constriction velocity (Max_Constrict_Velocity, P < .001). Average dilation velocity was not significantly different immediately after injury (T1) but was disrupted (faster velocity) at the asymptomatic time point (T2, Dilat_Velocity, P < .001) and was no longer statistically different from baseline at unrestricted return to activity (T3, P > .5).

This prospective cohort study was conducted at The US Military Academy at West Point. Cadets underwent a standard battery of tests including Balance Error Scoring System, Sports Concussion Assessment Tool Fifth Edition Symptom Survey, Standard Assessment of Concussion, and measure of pupillary responses. Cadets who sustained an mTBI during training events or sports were evaluated with the same battery of tests and pupillometry within 48 hours of the injury (T1), at the initiation of a graded return to activity protocol (T2), and at unrestricted return to activity (T3).
Pupillary light reflex metrics were obtained in 1300 cadets at baseline. During the study period, 68 cadets sustained mTBIs.

The clinical parameters showed normalization at time points T2 and T3. The pupillary responses demonstrated a pattern of significant change that returned to normal for several measures, including the difference between the constricted and initial pupillary diameter (T1 P < .001, T2 P < .05), dilation velocity (T1 P < .01, T2 P < .001), and percent of pupillary constriction (T1 P < .05). In addition, a combination of dilation velocity and maximum constriction velocity demonstrates moderate prediction ability regarding who can return to duty before or after 21 days (area under the curve = 0.71, 95% CI [0.56-0.86]).

Quantitative pupillometry as a biomarker for prediction of return to play in mild traumatic brain injury: a Military Traumatic Brain Injury Initiative study
Bradley A. Dengler MD, Melissa Meister MD, Michael Aderman MS, ATC, Steven R. Malvasi MS, ATC, Jeremy D. Ross MS, ATC, Adele Fu MPH, Thaddeus Haight PhD, Viktor Bartanusz MD, PhD, Jason H. Boulter MD, Jackson Rudolph BS, and Kenneth L. Cameron PhD, MPH, ATC
View More
Page Range: E12
Volume/Issue: Volume 57: Issue 1
DOI link: https://doi.org/10.3171/2024.4.FOCUS24140

The study was conducted from August 2021 to December 2022 at the United States Military Academy at West Point and was approved by the Institutional Review Board at Naval Medical Center Portsmouth. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to data collection. Freshmen cadets were recruited during the first 2 weeks of the academic year, and baseline concussion assessments were conducted at the time of consent. Participants were followed from the time of consent until the end of the follow-up period to document incident cases of mTBI in the cohort. This study followed the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines for cohort studies.

quotes.section: Methods / Pupillometry Parameters and Time to Return to Duty
quotes.quote: In a previous study, 3 of 9 pupillary measures (End-Initial, MCV, ADV) correlated significantly with the dichotomized (< 21 days or ≥ 21 days) time of recovery after concussion (B.A. Dengler, unpublished data, December 2023). Therefore, the goal of the present study was to examine the individual associations of these 3 pupillometry parameters with time to return to duty (Time_to_RTD), as a further refinement of the previously submitted analysis.

Participants whose Time_to_RTD was within 2 months (mean ± SD [range] 23.4 ± 12.7 [4–59] days) represented 94% of the sample (n = 64/68) compared with 4 individuals (6%) whose Time_to_RTD exceeded 2 months (range [61–71] days). Three individuals with Time_to_RTD > 100 days, for whom the expected delay in return to duty was due to other clinical considerations, were excluded.

This study reflects a deeper analysis of our previous work evaluating the overall pupillary light reflex after concussion, which is pending publication and demonstrated significant changes in the pupillary light reflex after mTBI along with an ability to dichotomize cadets returning to play or duty before or after 21 days. This study is a further refinement of those data, specifically examining 3 pupillary parameters that correlated with return to play and breaking them up into a more predictive model.
Of the 1,197 participants baselined, 514 cadets (131 female; 18.91 ± 0.96 years) consented and completed a valid baseline pupillometric assessment.
Freshmen entering a U.S. Service Academy completed a quantitative pupillometric assessment in conjunction with baseline concussion testing.
The purpose of this study was to report normative values for eight PLR measurements among healthy service academy cadets based on sex, age, sleep, race, ethnicity, anisocoria, and concussion history.

quotes.section: Master abstract / Design, setting, and participants
quotes.quote: Prospective cohort of adolescent athletes between ages 12 and 18 years recruited between August 1, 2017, and December 31, 2018. The study took place at a specialty concussion program and private suburban high school and included healthy control individuals (n = 134) and athletes with a diagnosis of sport-related concussion (SRC) (n = 98). Analysis was completed June 30, 2020.

We performed a retrospective clinical review of the PLR of patients attended in neurological clinics in our network over the calendar year 1 January 2019 to 1 January 2020 using the BrightLamp Reflex iPhone app.
